extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, especially new novelists and authors preparing/manuscripting novels
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to punctuate and format spoken dialogue in a novel manuscript, covering quotation marks, paragraphing, indentation, tags/action beats, interruptions, trailing-off, and handling digital/text-message dialogue. Aimed at authors preparing submissions or self-published manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation marks for dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue in your novel should be enclosed within quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All of the speech is contained within these quotation marks. This includes punctuation that is part of that speech (like the question mark). Example: "Hello! What brings you here?" she said.

rubrics_metrics.name: UK vs US quotation style (single vs double)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of single or double quotation marks largely depends on whether you’re writing in UK or US English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UK commonly uses single quotes: 'Like this!' while US usually uses doubles: "Like this!". The publisher's or editor's style manual will determine final consistency, but authors should pick one consistent approach for their draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start a new paragraph for each speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: For every new speaker, begin a new paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is crucial for clarity so readers can easily tell which character is speaking. Example: "What are you doing?" she asked. "I really don't want to see you right now." "I had to come," he answered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indent the first line of each dialogue paragraph (except chapter/scene starts)
rubrics_metrics.description: In fiction, every paragraph except the one at the start of a chapter or scene should be indented, including dialogue paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each new line of dialogue, even single-line ones, is indented. Exception: the very first paragraph of a chapter or scene is not indented (even if it is dialogue). See manuscript templates or publisher formatting for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place punctuation that belongs to dialogue inside the quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: If the punctuation belongs to the dialogue, it goes inside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question marks and exclamation marks that are part of the spoken line sit inside the quotes: "Why are you crying?" she asked. "I'm not crying!" he snapped back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a comma inside quotation marks before a dialogue tag
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use a dialogue tag (e.g., she said, he asked), place a comma inside the quotation marks before the tag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "I'm not sure what I'm doing," she said. This signals the speech continues into the tag.

rubrics_metrics.name: If there is no dialogue tag, end the dialogue with a period inside the quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: When dialogue simply ends without a tag, use a period inside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "I'm not sure what I'm doing." Use this when there is no following 'she said' style tag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action beats act as their own sentence (no comma and usually capitalized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action beats (narrative actions identifying the speaker) are separate sentences and replace dialogue tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the speech with its closing punctuation, then write the beat as a new sentence: "I'm not sure what I'm doing." She bit her lip, as if trying not to cry. Note the beat begins with a capital letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ellipses for pauses and trailing-off speech
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character trails off or pauses during their speech, indicate this with ellipses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "I'm not sure…" or "I'm not sure… Maybe we could…" Use ellipses to convey hesitation/trailing-off rather than a full stop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate dialogue interrupted by an action using commas inside quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character performs an action mid-speech, use commas within the dialogue and place the action outside the dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Okay, here's the plan. I think we should go here, and," he rifled through the papers and maps, "if we don't find what we're looking for, we can move on." The commas keep the speech flow while the action sits between quoted fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an em dash for dialogue interrupted by another speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: If one speaker is cut off by another, indicate the interruption with an em dash at the end of the interrupted line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "I have no idea what—" "You never have any idea! That's part of the problem," she argued. Guidance also includes practical tips on inserting an em dash (keyboard shortcuts or copy/paste).

rubrics_metrics.name: When quoting a quote inside dialogue, use the appropriate inner quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character quotes another person's words inside their speech, use the inner quotation marks appropriate to your primary quote style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in double-quote prose: "Frankl said, 'Between stimulus and response there is a space.'" The inner quote does not need italics; single quotes suffice if the outer is double (or vice versa depending on UK/US choice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting treatment for digital/text-message dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting scenes that include texting or digital messages, avoid quotation marks and use italics for convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For drafting, italicize messages (e.g., Hey, u ok? she messaged) or label speakers with names. Final publication formatting may change (e.g., message boxes) depending on the formatter/publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the publisher/editor style manual for final consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Many punctuation choices have acceptable variants; the publisher's or editor's style manual determines the house style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an author, learn one consistent approach for your draft, but expect your editor to make things consistent and align with either UK/US norms or the publisher's preferred style (e.g., Chicago Manual of Style for US).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t obsess over occasional drafting mistakes—editors will help
rubrics_metrics.description: Early drafts need not be perfect; editors exist to catch and standardize punctuation and formatting errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You should learn one way to punctuate/dialogue to present a clean manuscript for submissions, but minor errors in an early draft are normal and can be fixed in editing.
